origin_region: Blended in Britain; the base tea is usually Chinese (Keemun), Ceylon or Indian black, and the bergamot comes almost entirely from Calabria in southern Italy
processing: A finished black tea is sprayed or tumbled with bergamot oil (or a bergamot flavouring) and re-dried; some blends add dried bergamot peel or blue cornflower petals. Traditionally the base was a Chinese black tea; most supermarket versions now use Ceylon or Kenyan leaf.
harvest_season: Not a harvest: blended year-round from stock teas. The bergamot crop in Calabria is pressed from about November to March, so natural-oil blends are made from that year's oil.
appearance_dry: Dark twisted or broken black leaf with a strong citrus-floral smell, sometimes dotted with blue cornflower petals.
appearance_liquor: Bright amber to deep copper, clear.
appearance_wet: Brown-copper leaf that still smells of bergamot.
taste_profile: Bergamot's bitter-orange, floral, slightly resinous perfume over a brisk, malty black tea; the best are balanced and bright, the worst are perfumed and soapy with a thin tea underneath.

brewing.notes: Just-boiled water, 3–4 minutes; longer makes the tea tannic without adding bergamot. A slice of lemon is the traditional serve and milk works if the base is sturdy enough. A second, longer steep is drinkable but thin. It is the base for a London Fog (Earl Grey, steamed milk, vanilla).

vintage_note: A blend made to taste the same all year, with no harvest year and a best-before of two to three years, though the bergamot aroma fades well within a year of opening, so buy small tins. What differs between brands is the base (a Chinese black is softer, Ceylon brighter, Kenyan CTC in bags harsher), whether the label says bergamot oil or just 'flavouring', and whether cornflowers are added for looks. The name is not protected, so 'Earl Grey' can be anything from a scented Keemun to a flavoured dust.
description:
Earl Grey is the most famous flavoured tea in the world: black tea scented with the oil of bergamot, a bitter citrus grown almost exclusively on the Calabrian coast of Italy. The name honours Charles Grey, the British prime minister of the 1830s, but the story that the blend was a gift to him from a Chinese mandarin is a legend, and which London tea house first sold it is still argued over.

The making is simple: a finished black tea is misted with bergamot oil or a bergamot flavouring and dried again. The quality lives in two choices, the base and the scent. A soft Chinese black such as Keemun carries bergamot gracefully; a bright Ceylon makes a brisker, lemonier cup; a tea-bag dust just provides tannin. Real cold-pressed oil tastes floral and slightly bitter, while cheap flavouring tastes of lemon sweets and lingers on the tongue.

Brewed three to four minutes with just-boiled water it is bright, aromatic and brisk, and it takes a slice of lemon better than milk, although milk is common in Britain. The usual mistakes are over-steeping, which adds tannin but no more perfume, and buying a blend so heavily scented it tastes like a bathroom. A good Earl Grey should still taste of tea underneath.

There is no vintage and no season; buy a small tin, check whether the label says bergamot oil, and try two or three bases to find the one you like. Lady Grey, with orange and lemon peel, is a Twinings trademark rather than a general style; 'Earl Grey green' and 'Earl Grey rooibos' are the same idea on other bases.

It pairs with lemon desserts, shortbread and strong cheese, and if you like the bergamot note, a cup of plain Keemun alongside shows you what the base is doing.
